column4: The ayah says God covers the day with night (يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهَارَ), repeating the section’s root for night as an enveloping cover.
Here too the night covers the day (يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهَارَ), another direct occurrence of the section’s night-covering root.
Night and day are repeatedly wrapped around one another (يُكَوِّرُ اللَّيْلَ عَلَى النَّهَارِ), extending the image from a garment to the alternating world.
David is taught to make armor that protects people from their own violence (لِتُحْصِنَكُم مِّن بَأْسِكُمْ), a direct bodily garment of protection.
David is told to make full coats of mail and then to do good; the ayah joins protective clothing with moral action, as the section joins garment and taqwa.
The earth puts on its adornment, its people think they control it, then it is cut down as if it had not flourished; this sharply stages ornament, false security and its disappearance.
What is on earth is made its adornment as a test of who does best in deed, making outward ornament answer to the inward measure of action.
People come to God alone and leave behind what they were given; this pictures the loss of worldly goods when the self stands exposed.
On the Day, wealth and children do not avail; this directly sharpens the section’s claim about wealth at the moment of downfall.
For those who disbelieve, neither wealth nor children will avail them against God, and they belong to the Fire; material support fails precisely at the section’s fire boundary.
The ayah repeats that wealth and children will not avail against God and places their owners among the Fire’s people, another direct reversal of wealth as supposed shelter.
The disbelievers will be unable to ward the Fire from their faces or backs; this states the limit of every bodily defense against the fire the section warns of.
The Fire’s pavilion surrounds its people, turning an enclosing cover into confinement and punishment rather than shelter.
The supplication asks God to protect its speakers from the punishment of the Fire (وَقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ), making taqwa’s protective root an explicit plea for safety.
Believers ask, “protect us from the punishment of the Fire” (وَقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ), matching the inner safeguard to the section’s fire scene.
The people of understanding likewise ask to be protected from the Fire (فَقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ), a repeated formulation of the safeguard named in the section.
The angels ask God to protect the believers from evil deeds (وَقِهِمُ السَّيِّئَاتِ), extending the section’s protective root from bodily danger to moral harm.
God binds the believers to the word of taqwa (وَأَلْزَمَهُمْ كَلِمَةَ التَّقْوَىٰ) after placing tranquility in their hearts, locating the section’s protective quality inwardly.
The ayah says revering God’s signs comes from taqwa of hearts (مِن تَقْوَى الْقُلُوبِ), joining a visible practice to an inward layer.
This neighbour supplies the exception to 26:88: what avails is coming to God with a sound heart, setting inward condition against wealth and children.
God is the one who enriches and grants sufficiency (هُوَ أَغْنَىٰ وَأَقْنَىٰ), reversing the miser’s belief that his own wealth makes him self-sufficient.
This ayah completes the accumulation that distracts in 102:1 with its endpoint, “until you visit the graves”; worldly abundance ends at death.
The garden owner’s wealth is ruined, and he wrings his hands over what he spent; the failed property gives a concrete counterpart to wealth that cannot save its owner.
After the speaker says in 69:28 that his wealth did not avail him, this ayah adds that his authority is gone, completing the loss of worldly support.
The God-fearing are placed in a secure station (مَقَامٍ أَمِينٍ), directly linking taqwa to safety.
The people identified as God-fearing in 44:51 wear silk and brocade; this ayah places clothing within the secure reward of the protected, rather than the failed worldly mantle.
Night comes over Abraham (جَنَّ عَلَيْهِ اللَّيْلُ) as he observes the star; this is a non-lexical scene of night enveloping a person, like the section’s night as an entered garment.
Daylight is stripped from night, leaving people in darkness; this gives the night/day pair a clothing-removal image complementary to night as covering.
The command to take one’s adornment at every place of prayer brings clothing into a setting of worship, a specific counterpoint to adornment carried as worldly display.
This neighbour to 7:31 asks who forbade God’s adornment and good provisions; it clarifies that adornment can be a divine provision even while the section questions reliance on it.
Horses, mules and donkeys are given for riding and as adornment (وَزِينَةً), making the section’s broad dictionary gloss of adornment concrete in worldly possessions.
People extract ornaments from the sea “which you wear” (حِلْيَةً تَلْبَسُونَهَا), a direct instance of beauty literally carried on the body.
Those who take protectors besides God are compared to a spider taking a house, the weakest of houses; the ayah pictures a shelter that cannot perform the protection the section assigns to taqwa.
Whoever has taqwa is given a way out (يَجْعَل لَّهُ مَخْرَجًا), a specific result of the inner safeguard that parallels the section’s promise of ease.
The opening ayah says rivalry in abundance distracts people; 102:2 names the grave as its endpoint, exposing the impermanence behind wealth as ornament.

The source section’s dictionary branch gives debt as a secondary sense of ridā; this ayah treats a debt as a specified obligation to be recorded, so the link is that secondary debt-as-mantle sense, not a Quranic garment image.
